_note: Research tier. Landmark studies with where they were coordinated. Every row cites its source. Coordinates are the lead institution, not where experiences happened.

studies.name: Dutch prospective study
studies.finding: 344 consecutive cardiac-arrest survivors; 62 (18%) reported an NDE.
studies.cite: van Lommel P, van Wees R, Meyers V, Elfferich I. Near-death experience in survivors of cardiac arrest: a prospective study in the Netherlands. The Lancet 2001;358:2039-45.

studies.name: AWARE
studies.place: Southampton, UK (15 hospitals in UK, US, Austria)
studies.finding: 2,060 cardiac arrests; 140 survivors interviewed; 9% met NDE criteria, 2% described explicit awareness.
studies.cite: Parnia S et al. AWARE: AWAreness during REsuscitation, a prospective study. Resuscitation 2014;85:1799-1805.

studies.name: AWARE II
studies.place: New York, USA (25 hospitals in US and UK)
studies.finding: 567 patients; EEG recorded during CPR; 28 survivors interviewed; 126 community accounts analysed for themes.
studies.cite: Parnia S et al. AWAreness during REsuscitation II: a multi-center study of consciousness and awareness in cardiac arrest. Resuscitation 2023;191:109903.

studies.name: Cardiac care unit study
studies.finding: 1,595 cardiac patients; 10% of those who had a cardiac arrest reported an NDE.
studies.cite: Greyson B. Incidence and correlates of near-death experiences in a cardiac care unit. General Hospital Psychiatry 2003;25:269-76.

studies.name: Southampton study
studies.finding: 63 cardiac-arrest survivors; 6.3% reported an NDE.
studies.cite: Parnia S, Waller DG, Yeates R, Fenwick P. A qualitative and quantitative study of the incidence, features and aetiology of near death experiences in cardiac arrest survivors. Resuscitation 2001;48:149-56.

studies.name: Childhood NDEs
studies.finding: NDE features reported by critically ill children; none among a seriously ill comparison group who had not come near death.
studies.cite: Morse M, Castillo P, Venecia D, Milstein J, Tyler DC. Childhood near-death experiences. American Journal of Diseases of Children 1986;140:1110-14.

studies.name: Gallup poll
studies.finding: About 5% of US adults, then roughly 8 million people, reported a near-death experience.
studies.cite: Gallup G, Proctor W. Adventures in Immortality. McGraw-Hill, 1982.

studies.name: German survey
studies.finding: 2,044 adults; 4.3% reported an NDE; content differed between former East and West Germany.
studies.cite: Knoblauch H, Schmied I, Schnettler B. Different kinds of near-death experience: a report on a survey in Germany. Journal of Near-Death Studies 2001;20:15-29.

studies.name: Australian survey
studies.finding: 673 adults; 8.9% reported an NDE.
studies.cite: Perera M, Padmasekara G, Belanti J. Prevalence of near-death experiences in Australia. Journal of Near-Death Studies 2005;24:109-16.

studies.name: NDERF survey
studies.finding: 613 experiencers scoring 7 or more on the Greyson scale; feature rates and tone. Thousands more accounts archived at nderf.org.
studies.cite: Long J, Perry P. Evidence of the Afterlife: The Science of Near-Death Experiences. HarperOne, 2010.

studies.name: Liège narratives
studies.finding: 154 written NDE narratives analysed for which features occur and in what order; no fixed sequence was found.
studies.cite: Martial C et al. Temporality of features in near-death experience narratives. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 2017;11:311.

studies.name: Indian cases
studies.finding: 16 cases; messengers, a clerk with records, and being sent back as the wrong person; no tunnel.
studies.cite: Pasricha S, Stevenson I. Near-death experiences in India: a preliminary report. Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease 1986;174:165-70.
studies.type_label: Summoned by mistake and sent back

studies.name: Life After Life interviews
studies.finding: About 150 interviews that named the phenomenon and listed its recurring elements.
studies.cite: Moody R. Life After Life. Mockingbird Books, 1975.

studies.name: Life at Death
studies.finding: 102 people who came close to death; the five-stage model (peace, body separation, darkness, light, entering the light).
studies.cite: Ring K. Life at Death: A Scientific Investigation of the Near-Death Experience. Coward, McCann & Geoghegan, 1980.

studies.name: Distressing narratives
studies.finding: Of 123 written narratives, 17 (14%) were distressing: 8 inverse, 8 hellish, 1 void.
studies.cite: Cassol H, Martial C, Annen J, et al. A systematic analysis of distressing near-death experience accounts. Memory 2019;27:1122-29.

studies.name: NDERF overview of elements
studies.finding: Lists hearing distinctive sounds among the recurring elements: 'pleasant, musical, buzzing or ringing'. No percentage given.
studies.cite: Near-Death Experience Research Foundation. NDE Overview.

studies.name: Tibetan delok accounts
studies.finding: Deloks ('those who return from death') are people taken for dead who revive and describe a journey through Buddhist afterlife realms. Bailey compared these accounts with Western NDEs: no tunnel, and the judgment and life review appear as a mirror or a record read aloud by others, not as a private replay.
studies.cite: Bailey LW. A 'little death': the near-death experience and Tibetan delogs. Journal of Near-Death Studies 2001;19:139-59.
studies.type_label: A guided tour of the realms

studies.name: The Myth of Er
studies.finding: The oldest surviving Western account. Er, a soldier killed in battle, revives on his funeral pyre on the twelfth day and describes leaving the body, a journey to a place of judgment, souls choosing their next lives, and being sent back to tell what he saw.
studies.cite: Plato. Republic, Book X, c. 380 BC.
studies.type_label: Judged and sent back as a messenger

studies.name: Gregory the Great's Dialogues
studies.finding: Three accounts of ordinary people taken for dead who revived. In the best known, Stephen is told he was summoned by mistake, the wrong man of the same name, and is sent back: the same clerical-error motif found in Indian cases fourteen centuries later.
studies.cite: Gregory the Great. Dialogues, Book IV, c. 593. Discussed in Zaleski C, Otherworld Journeys, Oxford University Press, 1987.
studies.type_label: Summoned by mistake and sent back

studies.name: The Vision of Drythelm
studies.finding: Bede records a Northumbrian man who died of illness, revived the next morning, and described being led by a guide in shining robes through places of punishment and of light, then sent back. He gave away his property and lived as a monk afterwards.
studies.cite: Bede. Ecclesiastical History of the English People, Book V, c. 731. Discussed in Zaleski C, Otherworld Journeys, Oxford University Press, 1987.
studies.type_label: A guided tour of the realms

studies.name: The Vision of Tundale
studies.finding: An Irish knight lies as dead for three days, is guided through the otherworld by his guardian angel, and returns changed. One of the most widely copied of the medieval otherworld journeys, translated into fifteen languages.
studies.cite: Marcus of Regensburg. Visio Tnugdali, 1149. Discussed in Zaleski C, Otherworld Journeys, Oxford University Press, 1987.
studies.type_label: A guided tour of the realms

studies.name: Beaufort's drowning
studies.finding: Francis Beaufort, then a midshipman of 17, fell into Portsmouth harbour and nearly drowned. His account, written in 1825 and published in 1847, describes no pain, calm, and 'every incident of my past life' passing before him: the first detailed first-person life review in English.
studies.cite: Beaufort F. Letter to Dr W. H. Wollaston, written 1825, published 1847.
studies.type_label: Calm and a life review, without a journey

studies.name: Heim's falls
studies.finding: The first systematic collection. Albert Heim, a geologist, survived a fall in the Alps and spent 25 years gathering accounts from climbers, soldiers and workers who had fallen. He found about 95% felt no pain or fear, but calm, speeded thought and a review of their lives.
studies.cite: Heim A. Notizen uber den Tod durch Absturz. Jahrbuch des Schweizer Alpenclub 1892;27:327-37. Translated by Noyes R, Kletti R, Omega 1972;3:45-52.
studies.type_label: Calm and a life review, without a journey

studies.name: Otherworld Journeys
studies.finding: The scholarly comparison of medieval and modern accounts. Zaleski found the constants (leaving the body, a guide, a barrier, a return with a changed life) and the differences: medieval journeys are guided tours with judgment and punishment, modern ones are private, warm and without hell.
studies.cite: Zaleski C. Otherworld Journeys: Accounts of Near-Death Experience in Medieval and Modern Times. Oxford University Press, 1987.

studies.name: Tangshan earthquake survivors
studies.finding: 81 survivors of the 1976 earthquake that killed about 240,000 people were interviewed; 32 (40%) reported an NDE on the Greyson scale. The content differed from American and Indian accounts: mostly cognitive and transcendental features, and no tunnel.
studies.cite: Feng Z, Liu J. Near-death experiences among survivors of the 1976 Tangshan earthquake. Journal of Near-Death Studies 1992;11:39-48.

studies.name: The first medical account
studies.finding: A French military physician recorded an apothecary who, after heavy bleeding for a fever, lay unconscious and on waking described 'a light so pure and strong he thought he was in paradise', the most pleasant sensation of his life. The oldest known description by a doctor, rediscovered in 2014.
studies.cite: du Monchaux PJ. Anecdotes de Medecine, 1740. Rediscovered by Charlier P, Resuscitation 2014;85:e155.

studies.name: Chamorro cases, Guam
studies.finding: Four Chamorro accounts from Guam. No tunnel, no life review. People travel to another place and meet the dead, often along a path or across water, in a landscape that is recognisably their own island world.
studies.cite: Green JT. Near-death experiences in a Chammorro culture. Vital Signs 1984;4:6-7. Reviewed in Kellehear A, Experiences Near Death, Oxford University Press, 1996.
studies.type_label: A journey across a familiar landscape

studies.name: A Maori account
studies.finding: A Maori woman's account recorded by Michael King: she leaves her body, travels along a path to the north, meets relatives who turn her back, and returns. No tunnel. The route follows the traditional path the dead take to Cape Reinga.
studies.cite: King M. Being Pakeha, 1985. Discussed in Kellehear A, An Hawaiian near-death experience. Journal of Near-Death Studies 2001;20:31-35.
studies.type_label: A journey across a familiar landscape

studies.name: A Hawaiian account
studies.finding: An account from the early 1900s: the spirit leaves the body, travels, is met and sent back. Like the Maori and Chamorro cases, it has a journey and deceased relatives but no tunnel and no life review.
studies.cite: Kellehear A. An Hawaiian near-death experience. Journal of Near-Death Studies 2001;20:31-35.
studies.type_label: A journey across a familiar landscape

studies.name: Census of non-Western accounts
studies.finding: A review of every non-Western NDE account published to 2005. Two features recur everywhere: travelling to another realm, and meeting the dead. The tunnel appears in none of the accounts from China, India, Guam, western New Britain, Native North America, Aboriginal Australia or Maori New Zealand. The life review is largely confined to societies with a dominant historic religion.
studies.cite: Kellehear A. Census of non-Western near-death experiences to 2005: overview of the current data. Journal of Near-Death Studies 2008;26:249-65.

studies.name: Soviet resuscitation and 'clinical death'
studies.finding: Vladimir Negovsky founded reanimatology and ran front-line resuscitation teams in the Second World War, reviving more than 40 wounded men, some clinically dead from blood loss. He named 'clinical death', the reversible period without circulation. Mass survival of clinical death is what made modern NDE research possible; his own work did not record the experiences.
studies.cite: Negovsky VA, work from 1943 onward; see Safar P, Vladimir A. Negovsky, the father of reanimatology. Resuscitation 2002;53:111-13.

studies.name: Brazilian research centre
studies.finding: Brazil has the largest Spiritist population in the world and a long research tradition into mediumship, out-of-body and near-death experiences. The university research centre NUPES, led by Alexander Moreira-Almeida, reviews the evidence for consciousness surviving death. No Brazilian prevalence study is included here because none has been published with figures this atlas could cite.
studies.cite: Moreira-Almeida A, Costa MA, Coelho HS. Science of Life After Death. Springer, 2022.

studies.name: Enkidu's dream of the underworld
studies.nature: Epic poetry, not a personal report
studies.type_label: A guided tour of the realms
studies.finding: Dying of illness, Enkidu describes a dream in which a figure seizes him and leads him down to the House of Dust, where the dead sit in darkness wearing feathers and eat clay. He wakes and tells Gilgamesh, then dies. The oldest surviving text in which someone near death describes being taken to the land of the dead and comes back to report it, although it is a poem and not a first-hand account.
studies.cite: The Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet VII. Standard Babylonian version c. 1200 BC; earliest Sumerian poems c. 2100 BC.

studies.name: The weighing of the heart
studies.nature: Funerary text, not a personal report
studies.type_label: A guided tour of the realms
studies.finding: Egypt's funerary texts describe the soul travelling after death, guided past dangers, to a hall where the heart is weighed against a feather while forty-two judges watch and the person's deeds are recited. It is a guidebook for the dead rather than anyone's account of nearly dying, but the judgment scene is the oldest written version of a life being examined and weighed.
studies.cite: The Book of Going Forth by Day (Book of the Dead), Spell 125. New Kingdom, from c. 1550 BC.

studies.name: Odysseus among the dead
studies.nature: Epic poetry, not a personal report
studies.finding: Odysseus sails to the edge of the world and calls up the dead, who come to him in crowds: his mother, his comrades, the prophet Teiresias. He speaks with them, cannot embrace them, and is driven back by fear. Plato opens the Myth of Er by distinguishing it from exactly this tale.
studies.cite: Homer, Odyssey, Book XI, c. 8th-7th century BC.

studies.name: Nachiketa and Yama
studies.finding: A boy is sent to the house of Yama, lord of the dead, waits three nights without food, and is granted three boons. With the third he asks what becomes of a person after death. He is answered, and returns with the knowledge. India's oldest account of going to death and coming back, though it is scripture rather than a report of an event.
studies.cite: Katha Upanishad, c. 6th-1st century BC (dating contested; some place it c. 8th century BC).

studies.name: Aristeas and Zalmoxis
studies.nature: Reported as fact by a historian
studies.finding: Herodotus reports two men said to have returned from death. Aristeas of Proconnesus dropped dead in a fuller's shop, his body vanished, and he was seen alive elsewhere; his soul was said to leave his body and travel. Zalmoxis, a Thracian, vanished into an underground chamber for three years and reappeared, which convinced his people he had come back from the dead.
studies.cite: Herodotus, Histories, Book IV, c. 440 BC.

studies.name: Thespesius of Soli
studies.nature: Told as a real case by Plutarch
studies.type_label: A guided tour of the realms
studies.finding: A dishonest man named Aridaeus fell on his head and was taken for dead. On the third day, as he was being carried to burial, he revived. He described leaving his body through the head, seeing in every direction at once, meeting a relative who guided him, and watching souls being judged and marked by their deeds. He changed his name to Thespesius and lived honestly afterwards.
studies.cite: Plutarch, On the Delays of the Divine Vengeance, c. 100 AD.

studies.name: The Book of Arda Viraf
studies.type_label: A guided tour of the realms
studies.finding: A Zoroastrian priest is chosen for his piety, drinks a prepared mixture, and lies as dead for seven days and nights while his soul crosses the Chinvat bridge. Two guides take him through the star, moon and sun tracks into heaven, then down through hell. He is told to go back and report what he saw, and on waking he asks for food and begins to tell it.
studies.cite: Arda Wiraz Namag, Middle Persian; story probably of 9th-10th century Pars, text redacted into the 11th-12th centuries.

studies.name: Japan's oldest return-from-death tales
studies.finding: A monk gathered 116 tales told around Japan. Several describe someone seized by the messengers of King Yama, carried to his court, judged on a record of their deeds, and sent back, sometimes because the wrong person was taken. The same summons-and-clerical-error pattern found in India and in Gregory's Rome.
studies.cite: Kyokai. Nihon Ryoiki, compiled c. 810-824.

studies.name: Chinese return-from-death tales
studies.finding: An imperial anthology that preserved centuries of earlier Chinese writing, including many huanhun or 'returned soul' tales: an official or a daughter of a household leaves the body, is taken before the courts of the dead, has their record checked, and comes back. Many of the works it copied from are otherwise lost.
studies.cite: Taiping Guangji, compiled 977-978 under the Song, drawing on several hundred earlier works.

studies.name: The Apocalypse of Paul
studies.type_label: A guided tour of the realms
studies.finding: An expansion of Paul's single line about a man 'caught up to the third heaven' into a full guided tour: an angel leads him to see where the righteous and the wicked go, and what is done there. Zaleski treats it as the first of the four stages by which the Christian otherworld journey took shape, and it shaped every medieval vision that followed.
studies.cite: Visio Pauli (Apocalypse of Paul), c. 4th century, expanding 2 Corinthians 12:2-4. Discussed in Zaleski C, Otherworld Journeys, Oxford University Press, 1987.
